newsitem.title: USA: UPS strike ripples through economy.
newsitem.headline: UPS strike ripples through economy.

text.p: Thousands of businesses scrambled to get packages delivered Monday after the Teamsters went on strike, crippling operations at United Parcel Service.

Operations at the nation's largest package delivery service were paralysed after 185,000 workers walked off their jobs starting shortly after midnight. The strike began after last-ditch contract talks between the company and the International Brotherhood of Teamsters broke down late Sunday.

The strike left businesses across the country searching frantically for other ways to ship their products, supplies and vital documents. Given UPS' command of the package delivery market and rivals' inability to pick up the slack, many businesses found it next to impossible to send and receive goods and services.
"Yeah, it's had a negative impact on us," said a worker at Roxter Manufacturing Corp., a lamp maker in New York City. "We can't get our shipments out," she said.
If the strike drags on, its effects could start to ripple throughout the economy, analysts said.

"We'd probably start seeing some manufacturing shutdowns" if the strike lasts longer than a few days, said Michael Evans, an economist at Northwestern University's Kellogg School and a consultant for the American Production and Inventory Control Society.

"Facilities rarely have more than a couple days of parts and supplies on hand. If they don't get replacements in that time, we will see shutdowns," Evans said. "If this snowballs like that, we could see a substantial short-term dip in the economy."

No new talks were scheduled in the dispute, as Teamster President Ron Carey and UPS officials appeared to be digging in. President Clinton said he would not intervene after efforts by a federal mediator failed to avert a strike.

The union cited concerns about protecting jobs for drivers, package sorters and loaders from subcontracting, as well as pension benefits and health and safety issues. The company called its last offer generous and urged union leaders to allow a vote on the pact by rank-and-file Teamster members.
UPS is also a big customer of railroads and other shippers.

"There is the potential for a slowdown in intermodal traffic as the strike progresses," Salomon analyst James Valentine wrote in a report Monday morning. Intermodal refers to railroad cars carrying truck containers and similar combined modes of shipping.

Valentine said the big winners from the strike will be Airborne Freight Corp., Emery Worldwide, which is owned by CNF Transportation Inc., the U.S. Postal Service and RPS, a unit of Calibre System Inc.
But gains by UPS rivals could be short-lived, as the increase in demand has taxed their abilities to keep pace.
"We are seeing a dramatic increase in both inquiries and volume," Federal Express Corp. spokeswoman Shirlee Clark said.
"We're concerned that we don't jam up our system" by taking on additional volume, Emery Worldwide spokesman Rocco Sacci said.

Fedex, Emery and other UPS rivals said they would take on new business but only without disrupting service to existing customers. Neither Fedex, which is not opening new accounts during the strike, nor Emery could provide estimates of the amount of new business they are doing, or turning away, because of the strike.

UPS, based in Atlanta, said it was trying to ensure that blood, hospital equipment and other packages with critical supplies reach their destinations. It also said it did not expect its overseas service to be hurt by the strike.

The stock prices of several UPS rivals rose as investors bet those companies would prosper from the strike. Fedex rose $1.375 to $64.31, Airborne Freight added 81 cents to $48.56 and CNF gained 94 cents to $35.31, all in consolidated afternoon trading on the New York Stock Exchange. UPS is privately held.
